BST260 Final Project Proposal

Ziyi Wang

2026-11-18

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To: BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026

1. Project Overview

This project aims to apply statistical and computational methods introduced in BST260 to investigate two public health research questions using publicly available datasets. The project will emphasize reproducible data processing, exploratory data analysis, statistical inference, and interpretation of uncertainty.

Two analyses will be conducted. The first will investigate the association between body mass index (BMI) and systolic blood pressure using the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). The second will examine seasonal patterns in reported waterborne disease outbreaks in the United States using CDC outbreak surveillance data.

The analyses will be presented as two reproducible Quarto vignettes within an R package and published through a pkgdown website.

2. Vignette 1: Association Between BMI and Systolic Blood Pressure

2.1 Research Question

How is body mass index (BMI) associated with systolic blood pressure among U.S. adults, after adjusting for age and sex?

2.2 Data Source and Study Population

The analysis will use publicly available NHANES data provided through the R NHANES package.

The study population will consist of adults aged 20 years or older with available BMI and systolic blood pressure measurements. The unit of analysis will be an individual survey participant.

2.3 Variables

  • Exposure: BMI, treated as a continuous variable.
  • Outcome: Systolic blood pressure, measured in mmHg and treated as a continuous variable.
  • Potential confounders: Age and sex, selected based on their potential relationships with both BMI and blood pressure.

Additional covariates may be considered based on subject-matter justification and data availability.

2.4 Proposed Statistical Analysis

  1. Conduct exploratory data analysis to summarize the distributions of BMI, systolic blood pressure, and relevant demographic variables.
  2. Visualize the association between BMI and systolic blood pressure using scatterplots and fitted regression lines.
  3. Fit a simple linear regression model to estimate the unadjusted association between BMI and blood pressure.
  4. Fit a multivariable linear regression model adjusting for age and sex, and compare the estimated BMI coefficients across models.
  5. Report regression coefficients, 95% confidence intervals, and relevant model diagnostics.
  6. Examine potential nonlinearity and discuss the limitations of interpreting observational associations.

Missing values will be identified and summarized before modeling. A complete-case analysis may be used as an initial approach, with potential selection bias discussed. The need for survey weights and other survey-design adjustments will be evaluated according to the selected NHANES data and the intended scope of inference.

3. Vignette 2: Seasonal Patterns of Waterborne Disease Outbreaks in the United States

3.1 Research Question

Do reported waterborne disease outbreaks in the United States exhibit seasonal patterns, and are these patterns consistent across different historical periods?

3.2 Data Source and Study Population

The analysis will use CDC outbreak surveillance data available through the waterborne dataset in the finalproject R package.

The dataset includes reports from 1971 through 2023. Preliminary exploration identified 3,106 records with primary_mode == "Water".

The original unit of observation is an outbreak report. For the primary statistical analysis, outbreak reports will be aggregated into year-month counts.

3.3 Variables

  • Primary exposure: Calendar month, represented as a categorical variable with 12 levels.
  • Secondary exposure: Summer (June-August) versus non-summer months.
  • Outcome: Number of reported waterborne disease outbreaks per year-month, treated as count data.
  • Potential adjustment variables: Calendar year and observation time (number of days per month).

Historical periods will also be considered for stratified analyses to investigate whether seasonal patterns are consistent over time.

3.4 Preliminary Data Exploration

Initial data exploration identified 3,106 waterborne outbreak records between 1971 and 2023, with no missing year or month values detected in the selected records.

Of these records, 1,487 (approximately 47.9%) occurred during June, July, and August. July had the highest number of reported outbreaks, with 624 records.

Annual outbreak counts varied substantially across the study period, suggesting that temporal variation in reporting should be considered when interpreting seasonal patterns.

These observations are descriptive and do not establish statistical significance or differences in population-level infection risk.

3.5 Proposed Statistical Analysis

  1. Transform the original nested-list data into a tidy dataset and retain records classified as waterborne outbreaks.
  2. Summarize and visualize monthly and annual outbreak counts.
  3. Construct a year-month count dataset and examine the empirical distribution of outbreak counts, including the mean, variance, and frequency of zero counts.
  4. Explore the Poisson distribution as a candidate model for count data and assess its assumptions.
  5. Use a chi-square goodness-of-fit test to assess whether the observed monthly distribution differs from the expected distribution under a constant daily reporting frequency, accounting for differences in month length.
  6. Estimate the ratio of reported outbreak frequencies between summer and non-summer periods, together with a 95% confidence interval.
  7. Compare seasonal patterns across historical periods and consider year-level bootstrap resampling to assess uncertainty.

If appropriate, Poisson regression adjusting for calendar year and observation time may be explored as an extension.

3.6 Missing Data and Limitations

The analysis will distinguish between fields that are missing because they are not applicable to non-waterborne events and fields that are missing within the selected waterborne records.

The completeness and validity of year and month variables will be verified before analysis. Year-month combinations with no recorded outbreaks will be examined carefully before being interpreted as zero counts.

Potential limitations include changes in surveillance practices, reporting completeness, dependence among reported events, and differences in exposure opportunities across seasons.

Therefore, findings will be interpreted as patterns in reported outbreak frequency, rather than causal effects of season or direct estimates of individual infection risk.

4. Expected Deliverables

The final project will include:

  1. A valid and installable R package containing reusable data-processing and analysis functions.
  2. Two reproducible Quarto vignettes documenting data provenance, descriptive statistics, statistical methods, results, and limitations.
  3. Visualizations and statistical summaries illustrating the main findings.
  4. A publicly accessible pkgdown website hosted through GitHub Pages.

The overall goal is to demonstrate how methods learned in BST260 can be applied to real public health data, while clearly communicating statistical uncertainty, analytical assumptions, and limitations.
